 View Comments Dan Koh, the Sixth Congressional District's Democratic nominee. Jonathan Wiggs/Globe Staff PEABODY — Dan Koh, a former White House and Boston City Hall aide who eight years ago mounted his first run for Congress, will best Republican Micah Q. Jones in the Sixth Congressional District, the Associated Press projected Tuesday. The Democrat will become the first Asian American elected to represent Massachusetts in Congress. 
 Koh, 41, was heavily favored to win the Democratic-leaning district, which covers the North Shore and parts of the Merrimack Valley, after he emerged from a six-person primary field in September to succeed outgoing Representative Seth Moulton. 
 His victory was clear enough that he took to the stage to thank supporters at a Peabody event venue before the race was even called, or before Jones had conceded defeat. 
 “I want to be clear that I work for you,” Koh told a packed house at Olio Peabody, in remarks that focused on the shortcomings of President Trump’s administration. 
 “Let’s be honest: this is a scary time. We have a President who tramples on the Constitution every single day.” 
 The Sixth District was the state’s only open congressional seat on Tuesday’s ballot, where the rest of the state’s all-Democratic delegation was expected to win reelection. 
 Koh will enter Congress in January with deep Massachusetts political ties and a lengthy political résumé. He interned for the late senator Edward M. Kennedy and worked under former Boston mayor Thomas M. Menino. In 2014, at age 29, he was named chief of staff to then-mayor Martin J. Walsh. He previously ran for Congress in 2018, losing by 145 votes in a Democratic primary recount to Lori Trahan. 
 When Walsh became US labor secretary in 2021, Koh followed him as a top aide, and later worked for President Joe Biden as a liaison between the White House and cabinet members. 
 In this campaign, Koh leaned on his Washington connections, with Walsh canvassing for him on the North Shore and Biden and former vice president Kamala Harris making cameos in a television ad. 
 He was long expected to top Jones, an Army veteran endorsed by former Republican governor Charlie Baker. A one-time Democrat-turned-independent who registered as a Republican in 2022, Jones has described himself as a moderate, “common-sense” Republican. 
 “While tonight is not the outcome we had hoped for, I am incredibly proud of the campaign we ran, the coalition we built, and the message we brought to communities across the North Shore and Merrimack Valley,” said Jones in a statement released after 11 p.m. 
 Dan Koh campaigning in Lynn this summer. Josh Reynolds for The Boston Globe Koh’s victory caps a near-decade of angling for a congressional seat. After losing in 2018, he once considered challenging Trahan, but ultimately passed. 
 In the state’s 2021 redistricting process, Koh’s hometown of Andover was carved from the Third District and pushed into the Sixth, which Moulton has represented since 2015. Koh quietly considered a primary challenge, but the seat opened up when Moulton launched his own, ultimately unsuccessful, challenge to Senator Ed Markey. Koh was then among the first to jump into the race to succeed him. 
 During the campaign, Koh’s beltway experience became a target. One fellow candidate for the Democratic nomination, John Beccia, cast Koh as a corrupt politician, pointing to a report that Koh’s stock portfolio grew while he served in the White House. (Koh’s campaign said he did not buy or sell individual stocks during his time there, and Koh has advocated for banning stock trading by members of Congress.) 
 At the ballot box, such criticism ultimately didn’t matter. Koh comfortably won the primary, taking 41 percent of the vote in the five-way race. And in Tuesday’s general election, Koh won comfortably, winning more than 60 percent of the vote with 16 percent of votes counted. 
 On the trail, Koh ran on an anti-Trump platform, but also tried to avoid being pigeonholed, declining to call himself a progressive and saying he would “let other people label” him — even as he supports some of the left wing’s major policies, from realizing a version of Medicare for All to abolishing the federal Immigration and Customs Enforcement. 
 He’s also praised some of the country’s prominent democratic socialists while emphasizing he himself is not one. And he’s put little separation between himself and some more moderate stances espoused by the Biden administration on foreign policy. 
 Dan Koh, along with former Boston mayor Martin J. Walsh, Koh's wife, Amy Sennett, and their two children, on the campaign trail in August. Daniel Sarch for The Boston Globe He has criticized the Trump administration’s approach to conflicts in the Middle East, saying that “to basically just ignore the suffering in Gaza is a disgrace.” Yet, asked whether he believes Israel’s actions amounted to “genocide,” as many progressive Democrats have proclaimed, Koh demurred. 
 Koh, the descendant of Lebanese and Korean immigrants, hails from a family that includes a diplomat, influential medical doctors, legal scholars, and advisers to the powerful. He graduated high school from Phillips Academy Andover and holds two degrees from Harvard. 
 During his victory speech Tuesday night, Koh referenced his background and the journey of his forebears to the United States, thanking the crowd in Korean and Arabic. 
 “We will have failed if we go back to the status quo,” he told the crowd. “It’s time to help people as much as Donald Trump has hurt people.”
